items.title: Backdoor in Claude Code for VS Code extension on the Cursor Marketplace
items.content:
Phorion has detected a backdoor in the official Claude Code for VS Code extension bundle on the Cursor Marketplace that drops a persistent SSH backdoor across macOS, Linux, and Windows. This write-up focuses primarily on macOS, where the extension attempts to configure an SSH backdoor and establish persistence.

Organisations should immediately review their environments for use of Claude Code for VSCode 2.1.313 and engage incident response where use of the extension is discovered.

Phorion has discovered a compromise of the official Claude Code for VS Code extension on the Cursor Marketplace, where the backdoored extension bundle contains a persistent Secure Shell (SSH) backdoor. Cursor has removed the associated release from its marketplace, additionally pulling NPM and VSCode versions for 2.1.313 from their relevant registries.

While the implant includes setup and persistence logic for macOS, Linux, and Windows , we’re going to focus primarily on macOS in this post, calling out the key differences and a few implementation bugs on the other platforms along the way.

The Cursor Marketplace serves extensions for the Cursor editor. Because extensions run with the permissions of the IDE and the user running it, a backdoored extension gets immediate access to local files, source code, and developer tooling as soon as its module is loaded.

Notably, Phorion has discovered a likely oversight in how the malware tries to turn on SSH. The setup logic assumes it can check the current Remote Login state without root privileges. When run as a standard user, systemsetup -getremotelogin prints an administrator-access error and exits with status 0 instead of returning Off . Because the script only tries to enable SSH if the output matches Off , it skips the enablement step entirely. On a Mac that doesn’t already have SSH running, that mistake breaks the inbound access path, even though the SSH keys and persistence still get dropped.

In this post, we’ll walk through how the backdoor works, why that macOS check fails, and what to look for across your fleet. The goal of this payload is long-term interactive access, and whilst the SSH backdoor bug minimises impact on macOS, the malware is still a significant threat that installs persistence and beacons host reconnaissance back to the operator.

The compromised extension.js file starts with an injected immediately invoked function expression (IIFE) prepended to the minified extension bundle. The rest of the bundle looks like the standard extension, with Claude Code and VS Code strings, normal activate and deactivate exports, and UI code.

The injected prefix pulls in standard Node.js modules ( child_process , fs , os , path , http , and crypto ) and executes as soon as Node loads the file, before the extension’s normal activate callback even runs. The user doesn’t need to interact with the extension for the payload to fire.

First, the payload makes sure ~/.ssh exists and appends an attacker-controlled Ed25519 public key to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys , setting permissions to 0700 on the directory and 0600 on the file.

The key uses the comment svc-telemetry . Before appending, the script checks whether svc-telemetry is already in the file rather than checking for the key itself. When hunting for this activity, it’s worth checking the public-key fingerprint rather than relying solely on the comment string.

if (cur.indexOf( "svc-telemetry" ) < 0 ) {

Here, cur holds the existing contents of authorized_keys , and PUB is the embedded attacker public key (redacted here).

With the key in place, anyone holding the matching private key can authenticate as that user, provided SSH is actually running. The next step in the script tries to make sure the local SSH daemon is enabled and listening:

Linux: tries to enable and start sshd or ssh via systemctl , falling back to service and /etc/init.d/ .

macOS: checks Remote Login and, if it reports Off , tries to enable it via sudo -n systemsetup…

items.title: Statement: Denmark Continues its Work on Digital Sovereignty with Collabora Office
items.content:
Recent media coverage has raised questions about the status of a Danish government pilot project involving Collabora Office. We would like to provide some background, clarify what happened, and share our perspective on the continued work towards digital sovereignty in Denmark.

In 2025, the Danish Ministry of Digitization launched an initiative to explore alternatives to Microsoft productivity tools as part of its broader digital sovereignty strategy. The objective was not simply to replace one technology with another, but to establish greater freedom of choice and reduce dependency on individual technology providers.

The project was carried out in collaboration with the Danish software company cBrain , whose F2 platform is used across all Danish government ministries to support administrative processes, including case management, communication, document management, compliance, and archiving.

The first phase was successfully completed. Collabora Office was integrated with F2, demonstrating that individual users could freely switch between Collabora Office and Microsoft Office when editing documents, while maintaining their documents within the same government platform and using Microsoft-compatible document formats.

This was an important technical achievement, demonstrating how government organisations can introduce alternative productivity tools without replacing their underlying administrative systems.

Following the successful integration, the project entered a second phase, involving a larger group (around forty users) of ministry employees testing Collabora Office in their daily work.

As expected in a pilot of this nature, users identified functionality and compatibility issues requiring further refinement. Working directly with users, the project team collected feedback and continued improving the solution to address the specific requirements of Danish government workflows.

Initial issues with the pilot were leaked to the Danish press in December 2025. Senior Collabora Office engineers investigated and resolved the reported tickets. We were pleased to invest engineering and QA time in supporting the evaluation at our own expense, as we often do to serve our growing number of pilot accounts.

However, before this work could be completed, the Danish government was reorganised in June 2026, and the Ministry of Digitization was abolished as a standalone ministry. Its responsibilities and employees were transferred into a new ministerial structure.

As a consequence, the pilot lost its original organizational setting and was put on hold before the planned evaluation could be completed.

To our knowledge, no formal assessment of the final suitability of Collabora Office was completed, nor was a formal conclusion reached regarding the outcome of the pilot.

The interruption should therefore not be confused with a completed technical evaluation or a decision that the technology was unsuitable.

The interruption of the ministry’s pilot has recently attracted considerable media and political attention, including questions about Denmark’s progress towards digital sovereignty.

We welcome this interest in an important subject. At the same time, it is essential to distinguish between the interruption of an individual government project and the broader ambitions behind it.

The original technical integration was successful, valuable experience was gained through user testing, and the work provided a foundation for further development.

Most importantly, the underlying need has not changed. Governments across Europe continue to seek greater control over their digital infrastructure and the freedom to choose between technology providers.

We are pleased that the experience gained through the original pilot is now being carried forward through continued activities with other Danish public authorities, in collaboration with cBrain and its F2 platform.

items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 10개, 댓글 20개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 3일간 사용할 수 있습니다.

즐겨찾기 폴더 추가는 즐겨찾기 on 후 우측의 폴더 아이콘을 터치하여 추가할 수 있습니다.

items.title: The $6.3B Binance hack was pulled off in just 20 minutes
items.content:
Cryptocurrency firms and investigators are racing to freeze and track down billions of dollars of stolen digital cash following what appears to be the largest crypto heist of all time. On Thursday, starting at around 4pm ET, hackers started quickly siphoning around $6.3 billion in cryptocurrencies, spread across multiple blockchains, from wallets belonging to crypto exchange Binance .

Following the theft, Binance almost immediately suspended all deposits and withdrawals from its services as part of its investigation into the hack and says it is working to identify who was behind the breach. The company, along with other crypto firms, says it has so far been able to freeze around half of the stolen funds—essentially stopping hackers moving the money further or trying to cash it out. Much of the remaining crypto may not be possible to freeze, however.

Three crypto tracing firms have been quick to link the attack potentially to North Korean hackers. “We think North Korea is likely responsible,” Tom Robinson, chief scientist and cofounder of Elliptic, tells WIRED. “If North Korea is behind it, this one theft would almost double everything the regime has stolen in crypto to date.”

The majority of the stolen crypto was taken in a period of around 20 minutes on October 29, according to analysis by crypto tracing firm TRM Labs. Wallets belonging to Binance across at least ten blockchains—including Ethereum, Bitcoin, Tron and Solana—were drained and sent to multiple addresses controlled by a single attacker, according to TRM’s analysis . “Preparation began at least 36 hours before the theft,” TRM says in a blog post. The company says one of the attacker’s wallets received three small withdrawals during a test period, before later expanding the operations.

“Early on October 29, the operator deployed a first piece of code for the attack and tested it on two wallets,” TRM says. “Later that day, it rehearsed the final version on a third wallet, then routed the test funds back to itself. Four hours after that rehearsal, the same code was installed on a Binance hot wallet.” Hot wallets are cryptocurrency wallets that are internet connected and allow crypto exchanges to handle customer withdrawals. Analysts say the funds were drained from hot wallets across the impacted blockchains.

The tactics used in the hack appear to mimic previous methods used by an elite subset of North Korean hackers, known by the name TraderTraitor . Crypto tracing firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis both say they believe TraderTraitor may be behind the attack, while Robinson says Elliptic hasn’t specifically tied it to the group but sees overlaps in the activity.

Neither Binance nor law enforcement officials have named any suspected links between the attack and North Korean hackers. Over recent years, North Korean hackers have repeatedly targeted cryptocurrency firms and stolen hundreds of millions in crypto heists. Multiple North Korean hacking groups can target companies in the sector, but TraderTraitor have become specialists, pulling off infrequent but high profile attacks.

Within North Korea’s sprawling hacking operations —often designed to earn money for the highly sanctioned and repressive regime—TraderTraitor has stood out in recent years for its sophistication and targeting of crypto and decentralized finance companies. Last year, the FBI named TraderTraitor as being responsible for the $1.5 billion hack against crypto exchange Bybit.

Binance did not answer WIRED’s questions about whether it believes North Korean hackers are behind the colossal heist, pointing towards a statement saying it will cover all losses from the hack and is working with law enforcement officials to identify who is responsible.

Binance는 즉시 모든 입출금을 중단하고 조사에 들어갔으며, 다른 암호화폐 기업들과 함께 도난 자금의 약 절반을 동결했다고 밝혔다. 나머지 자금은 동결이 어려울 수 있다. 세 곳의 추적 업체가 북한 해커의 소행일 가능성을 제기했다. Elliptic의 Tom Robinson 수석 과학자는 「북한 소행일 가능성이 높다」며, 이번 한 번의 절도만으로 북한이 지금까지 암호화폐로 훔친 금액이 거의 두 배가 된다고 말했다. 사상 최대 규모의 암호화폐 강탈로 보인다.

items.title: Do At-Proto Users Know This Is Public?
items.summary: privacy
items.content:
I’ve been exploring the AT Protocol “atmosphere” that Bluesky runs on to get a better understanding of what people are doing with it. What I’ve found is a bunch of private data I’m not sure people know is public. Not only public, it’s easy to find.

To start my exploration I used two websites that catalog AT Protocol apps: atstore.fyi and atmosphereaccount.com . I’m a long time RSS user, so I got curious about feed readers first. I found this one called Skyreader and I noticed that their page on atstore.fyi contained reviews and mentions of the app by people who have used it. We’ll come back to this in a minute.

Something to know about Bluesky is that you can self-host what they call a personal data server or “PDS.” It’s where your data on Bluesky and other apps are stored, and it’s mostly public. Using a website like PDSls.dev you can explore it yourself. So if you wanted to see my data it’s here . I can’t control how or what you do with it, it just exists.

I didn’t want to authenticate my account with Skyreader without knowing what it would store publicly. So remember those reviews that people left for Skyreader on atstore.fyi? They’re all listed next to their account names, so I put their handles in to PDSls to get a sense of what would be public. From this I learned that each feed you subscribe to is published in the lexicon (what Bluesky calls an object of data with a schema) app.skyreader.feed.subscription which contains a key called feedUrl that contains the RSS feed. Cool, so now I know not to put feeds I don’t want my name associated with in there.

Without trying, I found someone’s private Club MacStories feed, which gave me full access to their content. With a little effort I found paywalled feeds for 404 Media’s full text feeds, Patreon backer exclusive feeds, and private RSS feeds for Gitlab repositories.

This led me to seeing what else someone could do with all this openly available data. So I investigated searching across a Bluesky relay (like bsky.network ) to pull down every collection record for app.skyreader.feed.subscription . It’s not as simple as one API call, because what this returns is an array of DIDs (decentralized identifiers) and from there you can look up the PDS server to request those collection records with the actual data.

This gave me over 1,300 RSS feeds people had subscribed to on Skyreader. No authentication, no real restrictions. It’s all just publicly available data on the internet.

It’s not just a Skyreader thing, I’ve noticed a few Discord clones store every message openly. There’s a Twitch clone that is the same way. I can watch as people chat all across Stream.place and even search the data. If you could easily search all of Twitch chat I think that would make some people sweat bullets.

I’m sure some people will say, “Sure, that’s the point,” but I’m not convinced the users understand the risk.
items.title_ko: AT Protocol 사용자들은 이것이 공개된다는 걸 알고 있을까?
items.summary_ko: 필자는 Bluesky가 기반으로 하는 AT Protocol 생태계를 살펴보다 사람들이 공개된 줄 모르는 개인 데이터가 쉽게 찾아진다는 사실을 발견했다. 예로 피드 리더 앱 Skyreader의 atstore.fyi 리뷰 페이지에는 사용자 계정 이름과 함께 리뷰가 공개되어 있다. 필자는 앱에 계정을 연결하기 전에 어떤 정보가 공개되는지 확인하려 했다.
items.content_ko: 필자는 atstore.fyi와 atmosphereaccount.com으로 AT Protocol 앱을 살펴보다가 RSS 사용자 관점에서 피드 리더 Skyreader에 주목했다. Skyreader의 atstore.fyi 페이지에는 이 앱을 써 본 사람들의 리뷰와 언급이 있었으며, 각 리뷰는 계정 이름과 함께 나열되어 있었다. 필자는 Bluesky의 개인 데이터 서버 PDS에 저장된 데이터가 대부분 공개되어 있으며, PDSls.dev 같은 사이트로 누구나 탐색할 수 있다고 설명한다. 필자는 공개되는 정보를 알지 못한 채 Skyreader에 계정을 인증하고 싶지 않았다고 밝힌다. 입력 텍스트는 이 뒤의 내용이 잘린 상태다.

items.title: Incident Report: unsanctioned agent behaviour during cyber testing | AISI Work
items.content:
You can access the full technical report here.

AISI’s role is to evaluate and understand the capabilities of frontier AI models, surfacing potential risks before they reach the public. To assess what these models can do, including whether they could be misused for cyberattacks, we test them under deliberately permissive conditions: with access to the open internet, and with some safety filters disabled.

On 28 th July 2026, AISI's Security Team detected unusual data transfers leaving our research systems during a routine cyber evaluation. On investigation, we found that some of the agents being tested had engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations. We declared a security incident and, within roughly one hour of discovery, had contained it and begun a full investigation.

The incident stemmed from a single evaluation where agents were given a task of solving a cyber security challenge. We ran this challenge 122 times across several models. Our investigation found that in 10 of those runs, an AI agent took autonomous, unsanctioned action on the live internet, targeting real people and organisations. In total, we catalogued 19 such actions. Almost all of this behaviour (17 actions) came from a single model, Anthropic's Mythos 5, with 2 actions involving OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Sol with cyber classifiers (mechanisms to prevent misuse) disabled. In the most serious case, an agent tried to insert malicious code into an open-source project. In an attempt to get the code approved, the agent engaged in social engineering  — creating fake online identities and using them to pressure the project's maintainer to approve the code. A human maintainer caught and refused to approve the malicious code.

These attempts were unsuccessful, and our investigations have not evidenced any resulting real-world harm. But this is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real-world.

Importantly, this was not a case of a model escaping its secure test environment, or ‘sandbox’. As was standard in our cyber testing, we had intentionally permitted internet access, and model-provider cyber classifiers were deliberately disabled - conditions that do not reflect how frontier models are made available to the public. We do this to best assess the maximum capability of models. These configuration choices have been common practice in frontier AI evaluations. The specific models in question, in the configurations in which we tested them are not commercially available and there is no clear indication of similar activity outside of testing scenarios.

Ahead of publishing this blog, we notified GitHub (the developer platform accessed during the evaluation) of the agents' malicious activity, which included actions that GitHub has confirmed violated their terms of service. We worked together with GitHub to remove artefacts left behind by the agent, and to notify the GitHub users the model interacted with. We have also contacted other affected parties. We also intend to work with METR (Model Evaluation and Threat Research) to conduct an independent third-party review – we are still working through the scope of this review with them.

This incident should be interpreted with caution and nuance. To some degree, our evaluation design choices and specific configurations enabled the behaviour. Nonetheless, the activity undertaken by the agent show signs of novel, potentially deceptive behaviours, and were to an extent and severity we did not anticipate.

There are important caveats to bear in mind: we observed a small number of events under very specific conditions, and cannot yet say how likely such behaviour is in different contexts or outside of testing environments. items.content:
The particles carry a customized dose of cancer antigens that can provoke a strong immune response against tumors.

The backbone of the vaccine is a modified, harmless bacteriophage called M13, which forms a nanofiber that can be coated with cancer antigens.

The backbone of the vaccine is a modified, harmless bacteriophage called M13, which forms a nanofiber that can be coated with cancer antigens.

A nanoscale particle with a unique structure, developed at MIT, holds potential as a customizable delivery vehicle for personalized cancer vaccines.

The backbone of the vaccine is a modified, harmless bacteriophage called M13, which forms a nanofiber that can be coated with cancer antigens. By precisely controlling the density of those cancer proteins, the researchers found that they could create a vaccine that prevents the development of colon tumors in mice.

This type of delivery particle could be adapted to carry many different antigens, allowing for the creation of personalized vaccines to treat individual patients’ tumors, the researchers say.

“The great thing about this is that it’s modular and we could switch out different antigens on demand, so you could design it to be patient-specific and target a known antigen for a particular kind of cancer,” says Angela Belcher, the James Mason Crafts Professor of Biological Engineering and Materials Science and Engineering and a member of the Koch Institute.

Belcher is the senior author of the study, which appears today in the journal Advanced Healthcare Materials . Shengnan Huang, research scientist at the Koch Institute, is the paper’s lead author. Jack Rudrum, Huaiyao Peng, and Hao Nghi Luu, graduate students at the Koch Institute, are also authors of the paper.

For more than 20 years, Belcher’s lab has been deploying the M13 bacteriophage in a variety of applications. This virus, which is harmless to humans, consists of a single strand of DNA coated in a protein shell, or capsid.

Belcher has previously developed techniques for generating materials by engineering these viruses to self-assemble into nanoscale scaffolds. By coating these scaffolds with inorganic materials, they can create functional devices such as  batteries , semiconductors,  solar cells , and catalysts, with precise control over the electronic, optical, and magnetic properties of the materials.

More recently, Belcher’s lab has been developing methods to control features of the phage that could allow it to be repurposed for medical applications, including vaccine delivery.

“We’re taking this toolkit that we’ve worked on and developed over decades and formatting it to be specific for vaccine therapeutics,” Belcher says. “Some of the lessons learned from making batteries and all these other things are now being fine-tuned to make personalized vaccines.”

The capsid that surrounds the M13 phage forms a long filament made from viral proteins. To create vaccines, the researchers modify one of these proteins, known as pVIII, by attaching an antigen to the end of the protein. This can be done by adding the gene for the antigen to the virus’s DNA.

Some of the lab’s previous work had suggested that changing the density of cancer antigens attached to the capsid could affect the strength of the resulting immune response. In the new study, Huang wanted to find a way to control that density.

“The antigen is the specific target we want to initiate the immune response against, which means we have to ensure the right dose of antigen to make sure that we can have a strong immune response,” she says.

items.title: This Week in Plasma: An Avalanche of Performance Improvements and Bug Fixes
items.content:
This Week in Plasma: An Avalanche of Performance Improvements and Bug Fixes

Welcome to a new issue of This Week in Plasma!

This week the Plasma team continued to polish up Plasma 6.8, fixing many bugs. Most of the regressions reported in Plasma 6.8 have been resolved now, so the team moved onto older bugs and squashed a very large number of them! In addition, there are some nice UI and performance improvements:

The Power & Battery widget’s “Manually Block Sleep and Screen Locking” switch now synchronizes its state across multiple instances of the widget. (Christoph Wolk, KDE Bugzilla #527560 )

When Plasma is asked to load a third-party shell package with invalid QML in it, it no longer crashes in a loop, but rather fails to loads and shows you an error message indicating what the problem is. (Marco Martin, libplasma MR #1610 and libplasma MR #1617 )

When using the Window List widget, really long window titles can no longer push other widgets sharing the same panel off the end; now the maximum length is capped at a certain point, and the text elides. (Niccolò Venerandi, KDE Bugzilla #456148 )

Using the Kickoff Application Launcher widget’s “Switch sidebar categories when hovering over them” setting no longer unnecessarily changes the height of the sidebar list items. (Niccolò Venerandi, KDE Bugzilla #524003 )

The Folder View widget no longer lets you configure it to use manual positioning in cases where this isn’t actually supported. (Niccolò Venerandi, KDE Bugzilla #513880 )

If you use the Pager widget at a large size, the app icons it shows now grow when needed to fit better within their window outlines. (Niccolò Venerandi, KDE Bugzilla #518625 )

Discover now lets you share and copy appstream:// URLs for locally-installed Flatpak packages too, not just ones that were installed over the network. (Taras Oleksyn, KDE Bugzilla #459827 )

Pressing the “Full Screen” button on a website shown in the Web Browser widget now shows the content full screen, as you would expect it to. (Niccolò Venerandi, KDE Bugzilla #507460 )

The Timer widget has received a significant round of visual and functional polish to make sure it looks and works well at all different sizes of panels. More is on the way for this widget, too! (Christoph Wolk, kdeplasma-addons MR #1131 )

Windows marked as excluded from screencasting are now also excluded from the Task Manager widget’s tooltip thumbnails. (Ramil Nurmanov, KDE Bugzilla #516184 )

The Konsole Profiles widget now shows the default profile too, not just custom ones that you created yourself. (Niccolò Venerandi, KDE Bugzilla #465553 )

Panel tooltips throughout Plasma that only show a single label no longer use reduced opacity for the text; now this is only done for subtitles when there’s a larger title. (Filip Fila, libplasma #1611 )

Before After Tab buttons throughout Plasma no longer have a weird almost invisible background. (Christoph Wolk, KDE Bugzilla MR #519745 )

Fixed a bug that could make screens that powered down in an unusual way get stuck at 30% brightness (or a similarly low level) when they woke up again. (Jakob Petsovits, KDE Bugzilla #523988 )

Fixed three cases where Discover could crash while checking for updates. (Aleix Pol Gonzalez, discover MR #1200 , discover MR #1446 , and discover MR #1447 )

Fixed a regression that made notifications inappropriately appear in the top-left corner of the primary screen when configured to follow the Notifications widget while the only Notifications widget was located on a different screen. (Sven Muckl, KDE Bugzilla #525536 )

Fixed a regression caused by a Qt change that made text in the Icons and Text Task Manager widget elide too early. (Nate Graham, KDE Bugzilla #526972 )

Fixed an issue that made remote desktop sessions occasionally fail to start from Flatpak apps. (Matteo Beretta, KDE Bugzilla #527555 )

The setting to remember the active keyboard layout on a per-application basis now works on Wayland the way it did on X11.…
items.title_ko: This Week in Plasma: 성능 개선과 버그 수정 대거 반영
items.summary_ko: Plasma 팀은 Plasma 6.8의 다듬기 작업을 이어갔고, 보고된 회귀 버그 대부분을 해결했다. 이후 오래된 버그도 대량으로 수정했다. 위젯 동기화, 잘못된 QML을 가진 셸 패키지 처리, 긴 창 제목 말줄임 등 UI와 성능 개선도 함께 이뤄졌다.
items.content_ko: Plasma 팀은 이번 주에도 Plasma 6.8을 다듬는 작업을 계속했다. Plasma 6.8에서 보고된 회귀 버그 대부분이 해결되어, 팀은 오래된 버그로 관심을 옮겨 매우 많은 버그를 정리했다. 주요 개선은 다음과 같다. 전원 및 배터리 위젯의 「Manually Block Sleep and Screen Locking」 스위치 상태가 여러 위젯 인스턴스 사이에서 동기화된다. 잘못된 QML을 포함한 서드파티 셸 패키지를 불러올 때 무한히 충돌하던 문제가 사라지고, 문제를 알려주는 오류 메시지가 표시된다. 창 목록 위젯에서 지나치게 긴 창 제목이 같은 패널의 다른 위젯을 밀어내지 않도록 최대 길이를 제한하고 말줄임 처리한다. Kickoff 앱 런처의 사이드바 카테고리 전환 옵션도 함께 다뤄졌다.

items.title: 대기업 총수, 의장 경제문제 때문에 못조져 놓는다는 건
items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

items.title: No, npm, “estee” is not a typo of “testem”
items.summary: javascript
items.content:
No, npm, “estee” is not a typo of “testem”

So, alright, look, here's the thing. Storyteller has a really long npm namespace because “storyteller” is a really common word, and so “@storyteller/” was already taken (by someone who doesn’t actually seem to use it, which, if you’re reading this, I’m still interested in your namespace!). So we’re stuck with “@storyteller-platform/”, and that means our command line tool for book forced alignment is named “@storyteller-platform/align”, and so you need to run “npx @storyteller-platform/align --help”, etc, which is a handful!

And so we came up with a cute nickname, “estee” (get it? Storyteller -> ST -> estee?), and we were pretty happy with it, so I went to publish a v0.0.1 to npm so I could set up Trusted Publishing with our GitLab repo and then this happened:

403 Forbidden - PUT https://registry.npmjs.org/estee -

Package name too similar to existing packages espree,testem

... What? Too similar to... “testem”? I mean I can almost understand “espree”. I don’t actually see how someone could accidentally typo “espree” as “estee”, but at least they're similarly shaped. But “testem”? No chance, that is not a typo candidate for “estee”.

I mean it’s pretty clear what’s happening here. Npm is using a Levenshtein distance calculation and banning any packages that have a Levenshtein distance of 2 or less from existing popular package names. Levenshtein distance counts the number of “edits” needed to get from one string to another, where an edit is a single character insertion, replacement, or deletion. So to get from “estee” to “testem”, we have to make the following edits:

See? Levenshtein distance of 2. We used this for the first several iterations of the Storyteller algorithm, which needs to find where a given sentence lives in a transcription of an audiobook.

Here’s the thing: Levenshtein doesn't scale down very well. You can’t just set a single threshold for all input lengths, because as the length of the string approaches the threshold, the proportion of the set of valid strings covered by the threshold explodes.

Here’s what I mean. Say you are concerned with all npm package names with length 4. Npm allows the characters a-z, plus the symbols “.”, “-”, and “_”, so there are 29 possible characters in our alphabet. For a 4-character string, that gives us 29 4 possible names, or 707,281 possible names.

But what happens if you don't allow any names that have a Levenshtein distance of 2 from any existing names? How many packages can exist before you have to start rejecting all new package names? This is a little hard to answer completely (and we’re ignoring the fact that, because Levenshtein distance allows pure insertions and deletions, this also affects 2-, 3-, 5-, and 6-character names), but we can set an upper bound: 29 2 , or 841.

This is because, since Levenshtein distance allows a replace edit, you can get from a string like “abaa” to any string starting with “ab”. So once you have all 841 strings starting with every combination of the first two characters, that’s it, you’re done, no more names. That’s 0.12% 1 of the total name space actually available to choose from.

This is especially apparent when considering our backup name, “hoid” (get it? Hoid ? World-hopping Storyteller?). Here are the popular packages that npm thinks “hoid” might be typosquatting on:

It’s much longer than the first list. This is because of the string-length — 4 is so close to 2 that you can reach way more usable words from a given length-4 string with a distance-2 Levenshtein threshold

None of these look like actual typo candidates for “hoid”. They’re all at least 50% different from “hoid”! “gopd”? “ gopd ”!?

Also, this just isn’t a very good rule. Seriously, this rule would have banned the project “preact” from being created because “react” already existed. It would have banned “estree” (which I assume only didn't trigger on my “estee” attempt because it’s not sufficiently “popular”) from being…

items.title: Nature-Inspired Tech Prevents Microplastics Entering Atlantic Ocean Through Wastewater
items.content:
Home All News Good Earth Nature-Inspired Tech Prevents Microplastics Entering Atlantic Ocean Through Wastewater

The commercial scale filtering device – credit, supplied to WHYY as a courtesy PolyGone Systems

Princeton alumni have designed what’s called a first-in-the-world device to filter microplastics out of wastewater at scale, and it’s already been deployed in Atlantic City.

The large implant mimics hydrophobic plants found in nature, which completely shed water on contact but also attract microplastic particles.

With the water moved on and the particles thusly removed, they can then be easily collected and sent to a recycling facility for processing.

The Atlantic County Utilities Authority (ACUA) in New Jersey have said that it’s crucial for public safety that microplastics be removed from water through existing processing streams. Though no federal regulation exists mandating that utilities remove these contaminants, the ACUA isn’t waiting around for one to be passed.

Microplastics can easily accumulate in wastewater through washing machines, heavy rains, and littering. Most existing treatment facilities across the country will be streamlined for human sewage, solid matter, heavy metals, and other well-understood contaminants, but microplastics present a challenge for these systems.

“We’re discharging to the ocean. So, if we’re not removing the plastic that’s in our wastewater, we’re putting it back into the environment,” said Matt DeNafo, president of the ACUA. “It’s getting into the fish that we’re eating, even the water that we’re bathing. So, it really becomes an issue for human health.”

The ACUA has brought onboard PolyGone Technologies , a startup founded by 2 Princeton University graduates Nathanial Banks and Yidian Liu, as part of a 2-year pilot program to see if their large filtration system can clean up this source of pollution in the city of 40,000.

“I think this really marks a new era for treatment innovation, where we’re able to build very large, scalable systems that use a very small amount of material and very low energy to treat very challenging contaminants,” said Banks, co-founder and CEO of PolyGone Systems. “And, having the first system in the world for that in Atlantic County, it’s quite unusual.”

Laboratory tests showed that a prototype could remove 98% of microplastic particles from wastewater, and the pilot program will focus on replicating this efficiency at the commercial scale.

MORE MICROPLASTIC SOLUTIONS: 3 Teens Win Global Earth Prize for Inventing Tamarind Powder That Easily Removes Microplastics

Interestingly, WHYY reports that Banks and Liu are architecture students, and the latter admitted that the most enjoyable part of the whole process was designing the large device.

In 10 to 15 years time, society may be look back and see microplastics as the greatest environmental crisis of modern times. The mass deforestation of the industrial age can be reversed as trees are given a chance to regrow. As debilitating as the pollution of the coal-fired revolution was to both human and environmental health, its effects were comparatively limited to the vicinity of the coal mine and the coal power plant.

Microplastics, in contrast have been found anywhere researchers have cared to look for them—from the bottom of the Mariana Trench, to the summit of Everest, and inside every human organ from the brain to the placenta—in quantities surpassing a gram, or even more.

ALSO CHECK OUT: Teen Discovers Coconut Fungi Can Filter Plastic and Sunscreen From Sea—And Wins Science Fair

Encouragingly, the majority of humanity isn’t waiting around for someone else to solve the problem, and GNN has reported on numerous inventions, innovations, and successes in the field of microplastic filtering and removal.

For Liu and Banks, they’re also interested in scaling down their technology for residential uses, while eco-conscious California is also the home to one of their commercial scale implants.

items.title: Through Captain Jean-Luc Picard, Patrick Stewart taught us the measure of a man
items.content:
Patrick Stewart died yesterday, and for people of a certain age, a little bit of the future left with him.

For a certain, less-than-new generation of fans of Stewart’s 1990s television work on Star Trek: The Next Generation, there’s a sorrow that the man behind the larger-than-life Captain Jean-Luc Picard would be lost to a very real, very heartbreaking condition, Alzheimer’s and Lewy Body Dementia, according to his family.

Stewart, of course, was far more than Picard. He anchored the X-Men film franchise and was for decades a dynamo on stage. But there are reasons Captain Picard, commander of the Starship Enterprise, is the character he’s best known for. Over The Next Generation’s seven seasons, four movies, and a revival show —Star Trek: Picard — that ended just three years ago, he portrayed a model of what mature, responsible adulthood could look like for a generation of boys who were bookish, imaginitive, and maybe a little nerdy.

Two of the Globe’s dyed-in-the-wool Star Trek fans share what Captain Picard, and Patrick Stewart, meant to them.

John Hilliard: For a younger, and likely wiser generation, stanning a bald middle-aged English actor who played a French guy on a spaceship may be a questionable life choice. But here is the thing: What made Stewart resonate as Picard was how he rooted the character, as in the best of fairy tales, in emotional truth.

Jason Laughlin: I agree. Picard seemed as real as the complex characters that would start to populate prestige TV a decade later. But unlike anti-heroes such as Tony Soprano and Walter White, Stewart gave us a nuanced character we actually admired. He loved his job. He had passions like archaeology , Shakespeare , and music . He held to his ideals even when it meant terrible personal sacrifice.

In the mess of American politics over the past 20 years, there have been so many times I’ve longed for a Picard-style speech that makes right and wrong crystal clear.

“You know, there are some words I’ve known since I was a schoolboy,” Picard said when a Joe McCarthy-esque admiral began witch hunting on the Enterprise. “With the first link, the chain is forged. The first speech censured, the first thought forbidden, the first freedom denied, chains us all irrevocably.”

His character’s moral clarity, and Stewart’s conviction in delivering it, put an end to the admiral’s reign of terror. If only real world oppression could be dispelled so easily.

For decades, Patrick Stewart was a star of stage and screen, but no role defined him quite like the noble space captain Jean-Luc Picard of Star Trek: The Next Generation. STEVE FORREST/NYT

JH: Full disclosure : Star Trek is a show, which Youtube will prove, that leaned hard on latex foreheads and sometimes-flimsy production to tell stories of intergalactic scallywags known as Klingons and Borg, Romulans and Cardassians. Like free office coffee, it’s an acquired taste.

JL: One of my friends has a theory that if you didn’t get into Star Trek before you’re 18 years old, you’re never really going to get it.

To me, what’s so accessible, and radical, about Stewart, though, was his ability to convincingly portray vulnerability while still maintaining Picard as a credible leader.

One episode saw Picard return to his home village in France to heal from a traumatic assault.

At the conclusion, Stewart surrenders the control that was his character’s hallmark and falls into the mud, sobbing, over his failure to fight off his assailants. It’s a raw, real, depiction of a broken man. Stewart shifts from total collapse into slow recovery by reconciling with his brother. Grief is replaced by warmth, and Stewart sells it perfectly.

JH: Totally. He knew how to make that show work for him.

That’s despite an episode where he faces off against a giant, talking tar pit . Or the one where he sells eating a sandwich in the sci-fi version of the family station wagon. Or when he chugs Ecto Cooler (remember Ecto Cooler?) with a depressed Scotty , from…

items.title: How hard is it to check for whitespace?
items.summary: java, performance
items.content:
By Sergey Tselovalnikov on 30 October 2026

When looking through a piece of source code recently, I stumbled across this method from Guava – a popular Java library from Google.

As you might've guessed from the name, this method checks whether a given character is a whitespace character. Yet the code looks a lot more complex than a simple c == ' ' check. This made me curious and sent me down a small rabbit hole trying to understand where all this complexity was coming from. If you're curious how this code works too, this article is for you.

The first thing one needs when inspecting a function that checks whether a character is whitespace is to define what whitespace actually is. While the SPACE (U+0020) is probably the best-known whitespace character, it's not the only one. If you've been writing code for a while, you can probably name a few more – the non-breaking space NO-BREAK SPACE (U+00A0) , a tab CHARACTER TABULATION (U+0009) , a newline LINE FEED (U+000A) .

Well, there are more. Unicode defines a White_Space property that gives us a list of 25 characters. Here they are – meticulously copied ,

, , , , ,, , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , ,　 .

Each of these characters has a different purpose. FIGURE SPACE (U+2007) , for example, has the same width as a digit in a table, while THIN SPACE (U+2009) and HAIR SPACE (U+200A) provide progressively smaller gaps. NO-BREAK SPACE (U+00A0) has the width of an ordinary space, but keeps the surrounding text together when wrapping a line.

It's not always easy to tell whether a character is in the whitespace set from the name or by looking at the glyph either. For instance, ZERO WIDTH SPACE (U+200B) isn't a whitespace character at all. Despite the name, it's a format character that can indicate a word or line break opportunity without adding a visible gap.

There are also some less obvious members of the set too. OGHAM SPACE MARK (U+1680) can actually be rendered as a visible horizontal line. In Ogham fonts with a stemline, the space continues that line between letters (e.g. ᚛ᚆᚓᚂᚂᚑ ᚒᚑᚏᚂᚇ᚜), while in stemless fonts, it's blank. So even the assumption that whitespace must look empty isn't always true.

Having a single definition of whitespace is only useful if everyone can agree on it. But even within a single runtime, some libraries might disagree on what whitespace is.

Consider the NO-BREAK SPACE (U+00A0) I mentioned above. It's included in Unicode's White_Space property, but Java explicitly excludes it , along with two other non-breaking spaces. The javadoc usefully highlights that the method checks for whitespace according to Java , rather than according to the Unicode property we had a look at before.

Character.isWhitespace( '\u00A0' ); // false

But what about other runtimes? Looking at two more popular ones, Python and JavaScript, we can see that there isn't a single authoritative list of characters everyone agrees on. Python, for example, has a convenient str.isspace() method. And unlike Java, it considers U+00A0 a whitespace character.

So possibly Python just follows Unicode's White_Space property? Not quite.

The interesting one here is FILE SEPARATOR (U+001C) . It's an ASCII control character originally intended to separate pieces of information, and it isn't included in Unicode's White_Space property. So Python recognises 29 whitespace characters, rather than Unicode's 25.

JavaScript takes yet another approach. It doesn't have an equivalent of the Character.isWhitespace() method, but we can use the \s character class in a regular expression:

The odd one out above is NEXT LINE (U+0085) . Unicode explicitly includes it in White_Space , and Python accepts it too, but JavaScript doesn't. Instead, JavaScript recognises ZERO WIDTH NO-BREAK SPACE (U+FEFF) , which Unicode doesn't include in the set.

I haven't looked through any other runtimes, but something tells me the inconsistencies won't stop at these three.

items.title: Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs
items.content:
Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs

Carmaker points finger at an 'unknown' flaw as customer fallout continues

Nissan has joined the growing list of Oracle customers cleaning up after a cyberattack, warning employees that payroll records, bank details, Social Security numbers, and other personal data may have been stolen.

In a filing submitted to the California Attorney General on Friday, Nissan Americas said Oracle had informed it of "a cyber event" involving the personnel records of "hundreds of companies." The automaker said it later learned Nissan had been "specifically targeted" in the attack.

A notification sent to current and former employees, seen by The Register , says the company believes attackers accessed a haul of sensitive info, including contact and banking information; Social Security, Social Insurance, or other national identification numbers; financial and tax records; and dependent and beneficiary details.

Current and former employees in the US, Canada, Mexico, and Brazil may have been affected, although Nissan said it is still working to determine exactly whose information was exposed.

Nissan said it kicked off its incident response plan after learning of the intrusion, brought in outside security specialists, and has been working with Oracle while keeping law enforcement informed. It plans to offer affected individuals credit or dark web monitoring where available.

The company has also put a few extra locks on the payroll office. Employees can now access pay slips or update direct deposit details only from a corporate network or through a secure VPN, while Nissan adds extra identity checks before processing payroll requests.

The accompanying employee FAQ pins the incident on "an unknown vulnerability in Oracle's PeopleSoft software" and says the campaign is affecting "hundreds of companies and institutions." The document offers no clue as to what the vulnerability is, whether Oracle has patched it, or whether the compromised PeopleSoft environment was hosted by Oracle or by Nissan itself.

The disclosure lands just weeks after researchers linked the ShinyHunters extortion crew to a wave of attacks exploiting a PeopleSoft zero-day . More than 100 organizations and roughly 300 PeopleSoft instances were reportedly compromised before Oracle issued mitigation measures, with the gang claiming to have made off with HR, payroll, and other enterprise data.

Weak security means attackers could disable all of a city's public EV chargers

US regulator tells GM to hit the brakes on customer tracking

21K Nissan customers' data stolen in Red Hat raid

Porsche panic in Russia as pricey status symbols forget how to car

Oracle has said little publicly about the reported attacks and didn't respond to The Register's questions, even as organizations have continued to disclose being caught in the fallout.

Nissan has not confirmed that the incidents are connected, though its California filing lists the breach period as May 27 through June 9, broadly aligning with the previously reported timeline.

The carmaker didn't respond to questions about how many current and former employees are affected, when Oracle first notified it of the breach, and whether the compromise was limited to Oracle-managed systems. ®

items.title: Intel’s woes wipe out $1 trillion of semiconductor market cap in one day — PC market bloodbath leaves few chip stocks unscathed: $1 trillion in semiconductor market capitalization wiped out.
items.content:
Intel's shares plunged 30% on Friday, wiping out nearly $150 billion in market capitalization in a single day, the largest single-day loss in the company's history. The decline followed a disappointing financial outlook, largely driven by an anticipated drop of more than 20% in sales at Intel's client computing group (CCPG), the company's main cash cow. The declines quickly spread across the semiconductor industry. Although losses elsewhere were nowhere near as severe as Intel's, approximately $1 trillion in semiconductor market capitalization was wiped out on Friday, according to intraday estimates by Benzinga .

The PHLX Semiconductor Sector Index (SOX), which tracks the stock performance of 30 major semiconductor companies, is one of the key indicators of the industry's financial health. On Friday, the index plunged 9.14%, or 1,052.82 points, to 10,465.38 points as of 2:31 PM ET, as Intel's disappointing outlook triggered a massive selloff across the semiconductor industry.

Intel was by far the biggest loser, as other chip-related stocks, while Arm (-12.68%), AMD (-12.48%), Qualcomm (-12.14%), Applied Materials (-8.73%), ASML (-8.13%), Lam Research (-8%), Micron (-7.28%), and Broadcom (-7.1%) suffered considerably less. Then again, while Nvidia lost 5.66% of its market cap, this translates to around $270 billion, which is a massive amount of money. Paradoxically, Nvidia lost more market capitalization in absolute dollar terms than Intel.

Intel VP Robert Hallock sets Nova Lake expectations, teases return to Raptor Lake for DDR4 platforms

Intel's one-two punch plan in desktop CPUs is taking shape

Benchmarking AMD's BC-250, offering Steam Machine-like performance at half the price

AMD splits Zen 7 into three EPYC families for 2028 and starts selling server CPUs by the agent

In an unexpected turn of events, the downturn extended to server manufacturers and cloud giants too, as Dell (-12.67%), HPE (-8.10%), Supermicro (-6.96%), and Oracle (-6.88%) lost nearly 7% to 13% of their value. Reuters noted that investors increasingly question the scale of capital investments required to expand AI infrastructure as well as the sustainability of that spending.

Intel’s client computing and physical AI group (CCPG) generated $8.1 billion in revenue during Q3 2026, down 5% year-over-year and 9% sequentially. Weaker demand and increased competition reduced client processor shipments by 14% year-over-year, which was partially offset by a 9% increase in average selling prices. CCPG accounted for nearly half of Intel's revenue of around $16.5 billion and the company's main source of cash. As strong demand for server processors only partially offsets declining client sales, Intel guided its Q4 revenue to be between $15 billion and $16 billion.

Intel expects the client market to deteriorate further in Q4 2026 and into 2027 as elevated memory prices and shortages of other components impact PC prices and demand. In general, Intel expects the client PC market to decline 10% in 2027 compared to 2026, which will inevitably have an effect on CCPG performance. While Intel expects its data center business to continue growing in 2027, industry-wide supply constraints will limit its ability to fully capitalize on demand.

2026 has been a mixed bag for Intel so far. On the one hand, the company achieved its highest market capitalization ever — $673.43 billion in mid-June — on growing sales of data center CPUs, strong sales of client products, and a return to profitability (if the $12.5 billion non-cash accounting charge associated with shares issued to the U.S. government is excluded). On the other hand, the company's capitalization has dropped by nearly 50% to $338.91 billion since mid-June (with $148.68 billion in just one day), as investors began to realize that the performance of Intel's CCPG heavily depends on memory prices, as customers and businesses tend not to like overpriced systems. items.title: Raspberry Pi Zero 3 W & Raspberry Pi 4 Model A Surface In Linux Kernel Patches - Phoronix
items.content:
Raspberry Pi Zero 3 W & Raspberry Pi 4 Model A Surface In Linux Kernel Patches

Written by Michael Larabel in Raspberry Pi on 27 October 2026 at 03:53 PM EDT. 9 Comments

It looks like a next-generation Raspberry Pi Zero is about to surface, the long-awaited Raspberry Pi Zero 3 W. And in an interesting twist in these times amid high PC component costs and supply chain constraints, a Raspberry Pi 4 Model A.

Merged to the official Raspberry Pi Linux kernel tree are patches adding Device Tree files for a Raspberry Pi Zero 3 W as well as a Raspberry Pi 4 Model A.

It's been five years since the Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W was released with many wondering whether any successor would come, especially in more recent times with RAM pricing and supply chain bottlenecks. Well, given this Raspberry Pi kernel activity, it looks like it could be here soon. The Device Tree file for the Raspberry Pi Zero 3 W puts it as using a Broadcom BCM2711 SoC, the same quad-core Cortex-A72 SoC used by the Raspberry Pi 4. Nothing else yet too revealing about the Raspberry Pi Zero 3 W in that DT addition.

Then the other surprise is a Raspberry Pi 4 Model A. Raspberry Pi had the original Model A and then the Model A+ and Raspberry Pi 3 Model A+ versions as lower-cost, cut-down versions of the full-featured Model B single board computers. The Model A versions tended to be slightly smaller and lower power consumption but with less I/O capabilities and even foregoing Ethernet. But it led to a lower price point.

While Raspberry Pi 5 is the latest generation, with Raspberry Pi single board computers continuing to be challenged by the rising component prices throughout the industry, it would seem logical to make a Raspberry Pi 4 Model A to offer something to those not needing a full-featured, current-generation Raspberry Pi SBC and to be able to do so at a somewhat lower price point.

In any event with this DT merge to the Raspberry Pi kernel, hopefully we'll be seeing the new hardware announced and in the marketplace soon.

items.content: 🚨 CVE-2026-120114 📢 Source: Wordfence 💣 CVSS Score: 0.0 (NA) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: False The Debug Log Manager – Conveniently Monitor and Inspect Errors plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Stored Cross-Site Scripting via the 'message (and pageUrl)' parameter in all versions up to, and including, 2.5.2 due to insufficient input sanitization and output escaping. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to inject arbitrary web scripts in pages that will execute whenever a user accesses an injected page. Successful exploitation requires that the site administrator has debug logging enabled with JS error logging active, and that the attacker can obtain the publicly emitted dlmVars.jsErrorLogging nonce — which is broadcast on every frontend page — to pass the nonce check on the unauthenticated endpoint. 📅 Published Date: 2026-10-31T09:29:27.152Z https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-120114

items.title: Chinese Hackers Abused Google Workspace Rules to Steal Research and Defense Emails
items.content:
A China-linked espionage group hid inside North American medical, academic, and military research networks for more than a year, quietly stealing sensitive research and defense email.

The way in was a backdoor on their REDCap research servers that stole login credentials. The exfiltration was the unusual part: the attackers rewired the victims' own Google Workspace rules to copy any message matching their keywords to an inbox they controlled.

Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) laid out the campaign in a report published this week and attributes it with high confidence to a cluster it tracks as UNC6508.

The actor and its REDCap backdoor are not new names; Google first surfaced both in February , in a wider report on state-backed attacks against the defense sector. It did not name the victims, describing them only as multiple organizations across the US and Canada: clinical providers, academic centers, military health institutions, advocacy groups, and health regulators.

Google says it notified them and disrupted the group's infrastructure.

The entry point was REDCap (Research Electronic Data Capture), a web platform that hospitals and universities use to build and manage study databases. UNC6508 compromised externally facing REDCap servers.

Google has not pinned down the initial access vector, named a specific CVE, or listed the affected versions, though it saw the group probing older, vulnerable ones.

Around three months after getting in, the group deployed custom malware GTIG calls INFINITERED , which trojanizes REDCap's own system files and does three things.

The earliest known compromise dates to September 2023, with activity continuing through November 2025. Once on the server, UNC6508 ran internal reconnaissance and credential discovery, pulling database and service account credentials, then used those logins to move into the internal network and on to a domain administrator account.

Google does not spell out the exact path to that admin account. With admin rights, the group set up the exfiltration.

The exfiltration rode a feature that was already there. UNC6508 abused content compliance rules, a legitimate Google Workspace admin feature that scans mail for keywords and can copy or forward matching messages.

Similar features exist in other cloud mail suites. The group created a rule, misspelled "Patroit," that watched for nearly 150 keywords, search terms, and email addresses. When a message matched, Workspace silently BCC'd it to an attacker-controlled Gmail address, which Google has since disabled. No malware on the mail server, no separate exfiltration tool, no unusual network traffic. Just a built-in mail feature, turned to copy the organization's secrets to an inbox the attackers owned.

MITRE already catalogs email-forwarding-rule abuse as a known technique. What GTIG flags as new here is the use of domain content compliance rules to do it, a method it says it had not seen from a China-linked actor before.

The rule's keywords mapped to UNC6508's collection priorities: geo-strategic policy, military strategy and equipment, advanced technology including AI and uncrewed vehicles, offensive cyber programs, and medical research. One term stood out for its specificity, chikungunya , the mosquito-borne virus behind a 2025 outbreak in China's Guangdong province.

Start with REDCap. Patch externally facing servers and remove old versions outright, not just alongside the current build. REDCap lets legacy versions run side-by-side, and that is what enables downgrade attacks, where an attacker forces software back to a known-vulnerable release.

Then check the mail side. Review Workspace, or equivalent, content compliance and mail-forwarding rules for anything that BCCs or reroutes mail to outside addresses. Check admin audit logs for when rules changed, not just what they say now. Pull GTIG's published indicators and hunt for INFINITERED. items.title: Sam Altman Says Gen Z Are Lame for Not Worshipping AI: "They always want to go do the thing that was cool five years ago."
items.content:
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman sympathizes with Gen Zers entering the job market. It’s just unfortunate that the AI tools he’s responsible for ushering into the world are completely upending the nature of work and finding a job.

“It’s totally true that huge numbers of tasks that people do today will be done better, cheaper, and faster by AI — and completely differently,” Altman said in an interview with Stanford’s Graduate School of Business, as quoted by Fortune .

This, according to Altman, actually presents an opportunity. He argues that all the tumult caused by AI is a good thing, as it gives ambitious Gen Zers who are willing to embrace AI an opportunity to catapult their careers or launch a business.

“I think you want to be starting your career at a time of the highest degree of change,” Altman said.

He then dissed Gen Zers who aren’t getting with the times.

“My chronic disappointment with MBA students is that they always want to go do the thing that was cool five years ago and not do the new thing,” Altman said. “I think this is a great time to go do the new thing.”

But the interviewer pointed out the obvious flaw in Altman’s logic.

“So go do the new thing, even if AI is the cool thing right now,” she said almost incredulously, eliciting a roar of laughter from the crowd.

The thing is, AI isn’t that far away from being what was “cool five years ago.” The excitement that bubbled from ChatGPT’s release in November 2022, and the wave of AI optimism in the year that followed, feels like it happened a lifetime ago. After that, public opinion on AI quickly began to sour. Artists and tastemakers certainly didn’t embrace it. But businesses rapidly integrated AI tools in an effort to economize their operations, automate tasks , surveil workers , and justify layoffs .

In short, AI is no longer “cool,” if it ever was. It’s now an inescapable part of our reality. Basically every programmer uses AI at work. Jobseekers are interviewed by AI models.

It’s so pervasive now that even tech founders are getting sick of it; Paul Graham, the cofounder of startup accelerator Y Combinator, acted as a weathervane when he said that he views AI writing in the pitches he receives as a sign of laziness.

items.title: A Deathless Roguelike - Jack Turps
items.content:
In Love Me Not you are a flower that climbs out of a cave. The cave has been cursed by a witch, so the level is regenerated above you whenever you fall.

This is similar to the procedurally generated levels in infinite runners like Doodle Jump , except that instead of erasing the entire level on a failure, Love Me Not only erases the most recent sections. This style of level generation is novel to me. For the purposes of this post I’ll call it spool generation.

I quickly became attached to spool generation. Procedural generation has a special place in my heart, but traditionally it’s a one sided conversation. The level is generated and statically presented to the player. Spool generation opens a dialogue. The player can accept or reject sections of a level. Rise to a challenge or retreat. Surpass a difficult area and then see it erased.

At the same time, the generated spaces can be alienating. They are amorphous and struggle to distinguish themselves. They never feel homely or familiar. They can’t just be received.

I wanted to write a little bit about how spool generation was worked into Love Me Not .

I often simplify a player’s time with a game into a “novice period” and an “expert period”. These are usually characterised by different goals. In Love Me Not a novice’s objective is to escape the cave by any means necessary, while an expert’s objective is to escape the cave as fast as possible.

Spool generation had some natural effects on the novice period:

The expert period was more fiddly. Time attack is a natural fit for this style of game, but it makes spool generation irrelevant. Any kind of fall is going to jeopardise your personal best, so you’re better off resetting the run. You never see the level regenerate.

This made the mechanic feel like an onboarding novelty. I wanted to find a scoring system that could bring spool generation back into the decision space of an expert player.

Time freezes seemed to work. After you fall far enough, Lomen the Lizard spawns above you, marking your “best height” with her tongue. If you ascend back above the tongue then the clock is briefly frozen. The freeze gets shorter each time it is activated.

The time freezes created a new gesture. From time to time, optimal play requires you to intentionally fall, spawn the lizard, and quickly climb back up. Because the climb regenerates part of the level, deciding where to fall becomes quite a complex decision.

Here are some things I consider when deciding when to cash in time freezes:

The time attack now feels strange. Previously it had been a familiar meditative state, a pursuit of perfect execution. Now it’s more critical and reactive. I’m reading the layout of the level, plotting how I could move through it, and deciding if I even should.

Thank you for reading. I’d love to hear your thoughts.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

오디오 파일로 변환해서 켜면 키보드 치는소리나오는거 까지만 하고 더이상 진행이 안되서 접었는데 풀이하신분 있으신가요?

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 10개, 댓글 20개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 3일간 사용할 수 있습니다.

즐겨찾기 폴더 추가는 즐겨찾기 on 후 우측의 폴더 아이콘을 터치하여 추가할 수 있습니다.

개별 이미지들의 위치 변경, 삭제, 별칭 추가, 폴더명 변경을 할 수 있습니다

items.content: 🚨 CVE-2026-118599 📢 Source: fedora 💣 CVSS Score: 5.5 (MEDIUM) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: False A file overwrite vulnerability exists in Epiphany when installing WebExtension packages from .xpi files. In src/webextension/ephy-web-extension-manager.c, decompress_xpi_thread() used libarchive with archive_read_support_format_all() (and filters), so the installer did not require a real ZIP. A TAR file named *.xpi was extracted. TAR supports hard-link entry types; with Epiphany's archive_write_disk options (including ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_PERM), a crafted hard-link target can cause an attacker-chosen existing user-writable file to be truncated and overwritten with attacker-controlled content and mode bits, without a dedicated warning dialog, when the user installs or opens the crafted .xpi. This is related to but separate from the ZIP-slip path traversal fixed as CVE-2026-77679 (#2922 / MR !2143). Requirements: the victim must install or open a malicious WebExtension (.xpi). Affected: Epiphany >= 47.0 (WebExtension XPI install path). Fixed: https://gitlab.gnome.org/GNOME/epiphany/-/merge_requests/2248 (commit 0cc9ab55 — only enable ZIP format support). Upstream: https://gitlab.gnome.org/GNOME/epiphany/-/work_items/2988 Reporter acknowledgment: Fernando Munoz 📅 Published Date: 2026-10-31T09:29:37.264Z https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-118599

items.summary_ko: Fedora 출처의 CVE-2026-118599는 GNOME 웹 브라우저 Epiphany에서 .xpi 웹 확장을 설치할 때 생기는 파일 덮어쓰기 취약점이다. 설치 코드가 ZIP이 아닌 TAR 파일도 처리하므로, 조작된 하드 링크 항목으로 사용자가 쓸 수 있는 기존 파일을 잘라내고 공격자가 정한 내용과 권한 비트로 덮어쓸 수 있다. 피해자가 악성 .xpi를 설치하거나 열어야 하며, 별도 경고 창은 뜨지 않는다. 영향 버전은 Epiphany 47.0 이상이고, 수정 병합 요청이 공개되었다.
items.content_ko: 원인은 decompress_xpi_thread()가 archive_read_support_format_all()로 모든 아카이브 형식을 허용하면서, 실제 ZIP이 아닌 *.xpi 파일도 TAR로 추출한다는 데 있다. TAR의 하드 링크 항목과 Epiphany의 archive_write_disk 옵션(ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_PERM 포함)을 조합하면 공격자가 고른 기존 쓰기 가능 파일이 덮어쓰기 대상이 된다. 같은 날 공개된 CVE-2026-77679(ZIP slip 경로 순회, #2922 / MR !2143)와 관련은 있으나 별개의 문제다. 수정 커밋 0cc9ab55는 ZIP 형식 지원만 활성화한다. 본문이 잘려 있어 이후 내용은 확인할 수 없다.

items.title: My favourite PowerMac is a Nintendo Wii
items.content:
So today I reached a nice milestone in one of my projects: my work porting classic Mac OS to PowerPC systems with what I affectionately call ArtX chipsets (Nintendo GameCube, Wii, eventually Wii U; the GameCube’s Flipper integrated chipset was very much designed by ArtX as it was effectively finished when ATI acquired the company, and the Wii’s Vegas (and its later revision Bollywood) and Wii U’s Latte are effectively straight successors) reached the desktop for the first time, most likely the first time since the CHRP clone era that someone outside of Apple brought up classic Mac OS on a new system to the desktop. Despite still being nowhere near ready for a public release, I want to talk about the challenges I faced with this project so far.

But first, why port classic Mac OS to this hardware in the first place? I’d already ported NT of course, and during that work I acquired some PowerPC Mac laptops which I also ended up porting NT to, work on one port improved the others and so on. This got me acquainted with the classic Mac OS, and I fell in love with the jank as it were (hacks upon hacks upon hacks going back to the 1980s is something I’d definitely describe as “jank”). Not to mention the m68k part of the TBXI is called “SuperMario”, and was for the entire PowerPC era. I wonder if a developer was a fan in the early 1990s?

Also, for the record: I started this project on 2025-06-22 (when I forked upstream openbios), no kind of coding agent or LLM was used, all coding, reversing and debugging work done by myself. I do these projects for fun and to learn, if I used “AI” it wouldn’t be fun and I wouldn’t learn anything.

Let’s start with the initial boot. “New World” classic Mac OS starts out with a bootloader called the “Trampoline”, which runs on an Open Firmware environment. So I needed to port OpenBIOS. Luckily, around this time Goldfish64 had started his own port of Mac OS X to the Wii, and he’d made an OpenBIOS port that I could use some drivers from, although for various reasons I didn’t just want to use his port directly (which was only targeting Wii/Wii U, I wanted to target GameCube too). I also decided to reuse some existing code to make some driver development easier (specifically the display driver), and thus changed my existing NT ARC firmware loader to load a big endian ELF instead.

I needed some small number of disk drivers for initial bringup, so decided to port my two drivers for devices on the EXI bus (this is just Nintendo and Macronix’s name for SPI), the “SD Gecko” (which is just a straight through adapter for a GameCube memory card slot allowing for SD over SPI), and the “EXI-IDE” (my driver is actually not correct to real hardware, but to my inaccurate emulation in my Dolphin tree allowing for testing under emulator with the low level debugging support that implies).

I wasn’t sure what kind of on-disk format I wanted to use (these drivers on my earlier NT port ran entirely using disk images on a FAT filesystem, due to the requirement for compatibiltiy with existing homebrew loaders that load executables from FAT filesystems, but this would naturally be limited to 4GB images for FAT32, and later versions of classic Mac OS needed more), so for initial testing I just took the “Mac OS ROM” TBXI file and placed it directly on a FAT filesystem as \ppc\bootinfo.txt for OpenBIOS to load it on boot.

So with that I could get the Trampoline running. I decided that I should try and apply as many patches to the image as possible as close to run-time as possible, so mostly untouched existing CD images could be used eventually.

The first issue I had was that the Trampoline makes some assumptions of the physical address space layout that are not true for this system. The physical address of a buffer gets calculated as an invalid address, so I patched that to an address guaranteed to be valid, and also the corresponding code setting up the memory chunk list/page table entries for the kernel.

items.title: The support case of a customer who said that all they could see was a black screen
items.summary: historical, windows
items.content:
If you hold a PC’s power button for 12 seconds, it will turn off at the hardware level without notifying the operating system. This is a safety feature so that you can turn of the computer even if the operating system’s “Shut down” command isn’t working.

After eight seconds of the power button being held down, the Windows kernel realizes that the user is trying to do a force-power-off of the system, and it quickly takes a kernel dump that can be uploaded to the Windows Error Reporting service the next time you turn the system on. (Sometimes four seconds isn’t enough time to get enough information, and the kernel dump is incomplete. I believe that on Windows Insider builds of Windows, you get a message that says something like “Please let go of the power button so we can collect more information, and then we will turn off the computer.” This gives the kernel more time to finish capturing its kernel dump.)

These emergency kernel dumps are internally classified as “long power button hold” (LPBH) failures. One of the pieces of information recorded in these emergency kernel dumps is whether the screen consists entirely of black pixels. Those failures are sub-classified as “black screen LPBH”, and they go to a special virtual team for analysis. (I happen to be a member of this black screen LPBH team.)

Sometimes the problem is a broken video driver. Sometimes the video driver is doing just fine, but the desktop compositor is just handing black pixels to the video driver. Sometimes the desktop compositor is doing just fine, but nobody is drawing anything to the screen. And those cases are further subdivided further into cases like “there is nobody around to draw anything” or “the person who normally draws stuff is hung.”

Back in the Windows 3.1 days, there was a customer product support call that would today have been classified as a “black screen” bug: The customer reported that they turned on the computer, and Windows started up, but when the logo went away, all they saw was a blank screen.

After some questioning, the customer support engineer put the story together: It turned out that this customer really liked the color black, so they decided to set up a goth theme. They set the wallpaper color to black. They set the title bar color to black. They set the button color to black. They set the window background color to black. They set the window text color to black. Every possible color you could pick in the Colors control panel was set to black.

Once you get yourself into this situation, it’s hard to get out because you can’t see anything.

I don’t know how the customer support engineer fixed the problem, but I’m guessing that they booted into MS-DOS, ran EDIT.COM , and deleted the [colors] section from the win.ini file , thereby returning all the system colors to defaults.

items.title: HP Poly VoIP vulnerability sets the stage for executive voice deepfakes
items.content:
HP has released patches for a critical buffer overflow vulnerability in multiple IP-enabled conference phones from its Poly Voice line. The flaw allows unauthenticated attackers to obtain root privileges on the underlying operating system, potentially enabling them to execute other attacks such as eavesdropping on conversations and recording voice data for AI-enabled impersonation attacks.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-0826 , was discovered by researchers from security firm Rapid7 and resides in the code that parses Session Description Protocol (SDP) attributes when the Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) feature is enabled.

ICE enables VoIP devices to establish peer-to-peer connections using the shortest available network path. The feature is not enabled by default on HP Poly devices, and the company advises administrators to disable it if it’s not needed.

The flaw, rated 9.2 on the CVSS severity scale, affects all phones from the HP Poly VVX series, as well as the Trio 8300, 8500, and 8800 IP conference devices. HP has fixed the flaw in its Poly Unified Communications Software (UCS) versions 6.4.8 for the VVX devices, 8.1.7 for the Trio 8300, and 7.2.8 for Trio 8500 and 8800.

An exploit module targeting this vulnerability has already been developed and released for the widely used Metasploit penetration testing framework that’s maintained by Rapid7.

The exploit executes code as root on an affected device with ICE enabled by sending a SIP INVITE request with a specially crafted candidate attribute. This attribute normally contains a transport address that can be used for connectivity checks and is part of the ICE RFC8839 standard.

The buffer overflow bug is located in a helper function called ParseICECandidate in the polyapp binary that processes such requests on the device.

“The start of the function contains a call to memcpy , which will copy the incoming string line being processed into a 256 byte stack buffer,” Stephen Fewer, senior principal security researcher at Rapid7, said in a blog post . “No length check is performed to ensure the incoming string length is less than 256 bytes. Therefore by providing a candidate attribute whose length is greater than 256 bytes, a stack-based buffer overflow will occur.”

Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), a kernel feature that randomizes memory addresses to defeat buffer overflow exploits, is enabled on the device. However, the protection is not operating correctly on the HP Poly devices because it does not randomize the load addresses of .so (Shared Object) libraries.

These libraries, such as libc , are loaded by other processes, including the polyapp process, and because their memory addresses never change, they can be leveraged to bypass ASLR and execute the attacker’s payload.

“We create a ROP chain that will execute an arbitrary OS command via the system standard C library function,” Fewer said. “The accompanying Metasploit exploit modules source code details the entire ROP chain.”

Attackers have increasingly targeted embedded devices inside enterprise networks in recent years because unlike laptops, workstations, and servers, these devices are not monitored by endpoint detection and response (EDR) products. As such, they provide perfect footholds inside corporate environments that allow attackers to remain undetected for long periods of time and attack other systems.

In the age of AI these devices become even more relevant for attackers, going beyond corporate espionage by recording conversations or internal network pivoting.

“Attackers no longer need massive datasets to make use of synthetic speech tooling,” Douglas McKee, Rapid7’s director of vulnerability intelligence, said in a blog post . “In many cases, they just need clean source audio of the right person saying enough words in enough contexts. That has made executive voice data, call recordings, and live conversation capture far more valuable than many organizations seem prepared…
